options: Training as many different model architectures as possible simultaneously
Removing or changing exactly one component while holding everything else fixed, then measuring the effect on a result you care about
Running the same exact configuration multiple times with no changes
Only evaluating a model on the training set
questions.explain: An ablation study isolates the effect of one specific change — an architecture piece, hyperparameter, or technique — by holding everything else constant and comparing the outcome to a baseline.

questions.q: Why does set_seed need to be called identically before building each configuration in a sweep?
options: It isn't necessary — randomness doesn't affect ablation results
So that the only difference between runs is the thing actually being tested, rather than a different random initialization also contributing to the difference
To make the training loop run faster
To ensure every configuration gets the same final validation loss
questions.explain: If different configurations get different random seeds, any observed difference in results could be due to the seed rather than the change under test. Resetting the seed identically before each config isolates the variable you actually care about.

questions.q: What is the most common mistake that undermines an ablation study's conclusions?
options: Using too small a batch size
Changing two things at once in the same run (e.g. removing dropout and raising the learning rate together), making it impossible to attribute the result to either change alone
Logging too many metrics to an experiment tracker
Training for too many epochs
questions.explain: Conflating two changes in a single run means you can't tell which one actually caused the observed difference. A clean ablation isolates exactly one variable per comparison.

questions.q: Why might a single run's validation loss be insufficient to conclude that one configuration is meaningfully better than another?
options: Validation loss is never a meaningful metric
A single run is a noisy estimate; the observed difference might fall within normal run-to-run variation rather than reflecting a real effect
Validation loss can only be computed once per training run
Single runs always overestimate performance
questions.explain: Especially on small datasets, a single seed's result carries meaningful noise. Comparing results across a few different seeds per configuration, and looking at the range rather than one number, helps distinguish a real effect from random variation.

questions.q: What practical benefit does structuring experiment configurations as a list of dicts (looped over in code) provide over hand-editing one script repeatedly?
options: It eliminates the need for an experiment tracker
It makes each run's exact settings explicit and reproducible, and lets you sweep multiple configurations consistently instead of risking accidental differences from manual edits
It automatically improves model accuracy
It removes the need to call set_seed at all
questions.explain: Defining configs as data makes every run's settings explicit, auditable, and easy to iterate over consistently, reducing the risk of accidentally changing something unintended between runs that a manually edited script would risk.
